idiom_name: stateful filter: ordered pending set + expected-sequence cursor + gap policy
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep a pending set ordered by sequence number (or a small min-heap), a cursor holding the next expected sequence per correlation, and a release rule. On arrival, insert the message; while the head of the pending set equals the cursor, deliver it and advance. When the head is ahead of the cursor, wait until either the missing message arrives or the gap policy fires; the policy is a known sequence size or batch bound, a gap timeout (on which the cursor advances past the hole), a capacity eviction, or an explicit rejection of late arrivals. Decide the duplicates rule (keep first or last) and bound the buffer, then deliver into a channel that preserves order and has a single consumer. Scope one instance per correlation id, and persist the window if delivery is at-least-once and ordering must survive a restart.
code_sketch:
state: pending = ordered set keyed by sequence number (bounded), expected = next per correlation
on message m:
    if m.seq < expected: reject_old(m)                # late arrival policy
    pending[m.seq] = m                                # duplicates policy: keep last
    loop:
        if head(pending) == expected: deliver(pop(pending)); expected += 1; continue
        if gap_expired(): expected = head(pending)    # skip the hole (partial release)
        break
pitfalls: Waiting for a full batch in a stream whose sequence size is unknown stalls until the timeout fires; decide explicitly whether order matters more than completeness.
Sharing one window and one cursor across correlation ids turns unrelated streams into a single ordering problem with a single, oversized buffer.
On timeout the cursor must advance past the hole, otherwise the next message waits forever and the stall repeats at every late message.
The guarantee stops at the first non-order-preserving stage: a parallelising or lossy channel after the resequencer undoes the ordering it produced.
Rejecting nothing means a redelivered old message is emitted after newer ones; rejecting everything means late-but-useful messages are silently lost.

Wrong move: Leave a stream resequencer waiting forever for a missing sequence -> one lost message stalls the group and keeps the backlog resident -> instead set a timeout/capacity bound and route partial or discarded work for reconciliation.

Wrong move: Share one cursor across every correlation id -> unrelated streams block each other and memory grows with aggregate traffic -> instead maintain an independent bounded window per correlation.

Wrong move: Treat duplicate and late sequence numbers as ordinary arrivals -> retries can overwrite or emit stale data after newer messages -> instead detect them and apply an explicit deduplicate, reject, or dead-letter policy.
